lessons.unit: Unit 2.1: The nature of belief in Allah
lessons.title: What the Qur'an teaches about Allah: Ayat al-Kursi and the names
lessons.bigQuestion: How does the Qur'an describe the One we worship?
objectives: Identify characteristics of Allah shown in the Qur'an
Explain what each characteristic teaches about Allah
Show how these shape the belief and behaviour of a Muslim
successCriteria: All: name three characteristics of Allah
Most: link each to a Qur'anic passage
Some: explain how a characteristic affects a Muslim's life
lessons.crossCurricular: Literature: reading a sacred text closely
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder, gratitude and humility before Allah
starter: Name two attributes of Allah you know.

teach.heading: Allah in the Qur'an
bullets: The Qur'an begins by praising Allah as Rahman and Rahim.
It describes Allah as One, Creator, Knower and Sustainer.
Every surah (except one) begins with Bismillah.
teach.note: Open with Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim and ask what it tells us. The Qur'an teaches about Allah through names and descriptions; we use passages, not invention. Surah 1 praises Allah as Lord of the worlds, Rahman, Rahim, and Master of the Day of Judgment (verify 1:1-4). Surah 9 has no Bismillah at its beginning. Teacher note: every Qur'an reference here is marked verify; check the surah and ayah numbers and the translation against a trusted mushaf and translation before the lesson.

quote.text: There is nothing like Him. (Qur'an 42:11, verify)

teach.heading: Ayat al-Kursi
bullets: Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.
His knowledge and authority extend over the heavens and the earth.
teach.note: Teach from Qur'an 2:255 (verify). Paraphrase rather than quoting the whole verse. Points: Allah is al-Hayy, al-Qayyum; nothing happens without His permission; He knows what is before and behind people; His throne extends over the heavens and earth. Ask what this teaches about Allah's power and care. Avoid describing Allah in human terms; the Qur'an says there is nothing like Him. Teacher note: every Qur'an reference here is marked verify; check the surah and ayah numbers and the translation against a trusted mushaf and translation before the lesson.

teach.heading: Names and what they show
teach.note: Link to the previous lessons on omnipotence, Creator, Merciful and Just. Add al-Alim (All-Knowing), al-Hayy, al-Qayyum. Suggest the Qur'an passage 59:22-24 as a source of a list of names (verify). For each, ask how a Muslim responds: gratitude, trust, fear of wrongdoing, hope in mercy. Pupils must give a characteristic, an evidence source and a consequence.

head: Characteristic
What it shows
Effect on a Muslim
rows: Allah is ever-living and sustains all

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Show how a good 4-mark answer uses a point, a source and a link.

model.problem: Explain one characteristic of Allah shown in the Qur'an. (3 marks)
steps: Point: Allah is Al-Alim, the All-Knowing
Evidence: the Qur'an teaches that nothing is hidden from Him (reference to verify)
Link: a Muslim tries to be honest, even in private, because Allah knows everything
model.answer: Characteristic, source, consequence for a Muslim

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer A (option 1). The other options are from different surahs or unrelated to constant care.

check.q: Which phrase from Ayat al-Kursi shows Allah is never tired or inattentive?
options: Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him
By the fig and the olive
check.why: Ayat al-Kursi teaches Allah never sleeps or slumbers, showing constant care. The Surah 112 option is about oneness, a different point.

practice: Match each characteristic to its meaning: Al-Hayy; Al-Qayyum; Ar-Rahman; Al-Alim.
Write one sentence about how knowing that Allah is All-Knowing changes behaviour.
independent: Core: Name three characteristics of Allah shown in the Qur'an. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain two characteristics of Allah shown in the Qur'an and how each affects a Muslim. (6 marks)
Stretch: 'Mercy is the most important characteristic of Allah.' Evaluate this view. (12 marks)
exit: Why do Muslims begin with Bismillah?
lessons.homework: Learn the meaning of five names of Allah and write a sentence for each. Ask a teacher or imam to check the transliteration.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards for names. EAL: Arabic names with transliteration and translations. Stretch: compare two names that seem to point in different directions, such as Mercy and Justice.

lessons.title: Akhirah in the Qur'an: accountability, resurrection and the record of deeds
lessons.bigQuestion: How does the Qur'an make the next life real for the reader?
objectives: Identify the Qur'an's main teachings on death, resurrection, accountability and the final abode
Explain how particular Qur'anic passages express these teachings
Show how belief in Akhirah affects Muslim behaviour
successCriteria: All: describe two teachings about Akhirah that appear in the Qur'an
Most: link each teaching to a passage
Some: evaluate how far the Qur'an's style makes Akhirah vivid
lessons.crossCurricular: English: imagery and tone in scripture
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: accountability, hope and fear of Allah in balance

keywords.def: the scale on which deeds are weighed

starter: Name two beliefs about the Day of Judgment.

teach.heading: Where the Qur'an speaks of Akhirah
bullets: Akhirah is one of the most frequent themes in the Qur'an.
Many short Makkan surahs describe the Day vividly.
Passages stress death, resurrection and accountability.
teach.note: Explain that the Qur'an returns to Akhirah often, often right after teachings about tawhid, to remind people that actions have consequences. Link to the previous lessons on Barzakh, the Day of Judgment, Jannah and Jahannam. Stress we use only passages we can reference; mark these references for checking. Teacher note: every Qur'an reference here is marked verify; check the surah and ayah numbers and the translation against a trusted mushaf and translation before the lesson.

quote.text: Every soul will taste death. (Qur'an 3:185, verify)

teach.heading: Accountability and justice
bullets: Surah 99 teaches that even tiny good or bad deeds will be seen.
Every deed is recorded and each person receives a record.
Justice means nobody is wronged on that Day.
teach.note: Teach Surah 99 (al-Zalzalah, verify), especially verses 7 and 8, about an atom's weight of good or evil being seen. Paraphrase. Another passage often cited is 17:13-14 on the record of deeds (verify). Ask what difference this belief makes to small everyday choices such as returning a lost item. Teacher note: every Qur'an reference here is marked verify; check the surah and ayah numbers and the translation against a trusted mushaf and translation before the lesson.

teach.heading: Three groups and the final abode
teach.note: Surah 56 (al-Waqi'ah) describes people divided into groups on the Day (verify 56:7-10). Keep to a simple summary: some are foremost, some are people of the right, some are people of the left. Link to Jannah and Jahannam; the Qur'an uses vivid description of gardens and rivers and of punishment, and pupils should avoid adding details not in the text. Ask how fear and hope work together in a Muslim's faith.

right.title: Promises
points: Reward for believers who do good

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Show the P-E-E structure. A reference marked verify must be checked before an exam-style class uses it; in the exam candidates may paraphrase the meaning without the number.

model.problem: Explain one way the Qur'an teaches that Muslims will be accountable in Akhirah. (3 marks)
steps: Point: the Qur'an teaches every deed will be seen, even the smallest
Evidence: Surah 99 says an atom's weight of good or evil will be seen (verify 99:7-8)
Link: so Muslims try to do good in private as well as in public

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. A refers to Hajj. B is about charity. D is a different belief.

check.q: Which teaching about Akhirah does Surah 99 mainly express?
options: Even tiny deeds will be seen and judged
check.why: Surah 99 stresses accountability for every deed, however small.

practice: Give two reasons why the Qur'an returns often to the subject of Akhirah.
Write a sentence linking belief in accountability to honesty.
independent: Core: Describe two teachings about Akhirah in the Qur'an. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain two ways the Qur'an expresses accountability. (6 marks)
Stretch: 'The Qur'an's teachings on Akhirah are most important in guiding behaviour.' Evaluate this view. (12 marks)
exit: Name one Qur'anic theme about Akhirah.
Why do Muslims believe all deeds matter?
lessons.homework: Choose one passage on Akhirah studied in class, check its reference in a translation, and write 5 sentences on what it teaches.
lessons.send: SEND: card sort of teachings and passages. EAL: key terms in Arabic and English. Stretch: compare how Surah 99 and Surah 101 express accountability.
